## June 23, 1956 — A Saturday

You arrived on a warm Saturday in the middle of the American summer, into a world that was simultaneously more stable and more volatile than it appeared. The postwar boom was in full effect — new cars, new suburbs, new televisions arriving in living rooms that had never had them. But underneath that prosperity, old empires were cracking, a superpower rivalry was shaping everything, and a generation of young people was beginning to sense that the world their parents had built wasn't going to hold.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, Egypt held a constitutional referendum confirming Gamal Abdel Nasser as president with an overwhelming majority.

This was a moment of profound regional consequence: an Arab nationalist declaring that Egypt belonged to Egyptians, not to the European powers that had controlled the Canal and the country for decades. Nasser's political consolidation on the day of your birth was a signal of what was coming. Within weeks he would nationalize the Suez Canal and trigger an international crisis that effectively announced the end of the British Empire as a world-ordering force. You were born on the day a new world began replacing an old one.

The Montgomery Bus Boycott was entering its seventh month. Rosa Parks had been arrested the previous December, and Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama had spent half a year walking, carpooling, and refusing to board city buses. The legal battle was before the Supreme Court. The outcome was not yet certain. You arrived in a country arguing loudly, and sometimes violently, about whether its founding promises applied to all of its people.

Elvis Presley was twenty-one and had spent that spring reordering American popular music. "Heartbreak Hotel" had gone to number one in April. By June he was the most famous entertainer in the country, and the old guard of popular music didn't know what to do with him. Rock and roll was not a trend; it was a rupture.

---

**Within thirty days of your birth — one historically significant worldwide event:**

On July 19, 1956 — twenty-six days after you were born — the United States and Britain abruptly withdrew their offer to finance Egypt's Aswan High Dam. Nasser's response came seven days later: he nationalized the Suez Canal. Britain, France, and Israel invaded Egypt that October. The United States forced them to withdraw. In the space of a few months, it had been demonstrated conclusively that the old European empires could no longer act in the world without American permission. The British Empire, for practical purposes, ended in the season of your birth.

---

**The arc of your seventy years:**

You were a toddler when Sputnik crossed the night sky in October 1957, a blinking light that told the world the space age had arrived and the Soviet Union had gotten there first. You were seven when John Kennedy was shot in Dallas, an event that fractured something in the national confidence that never fully healed.

You were thirteen in the summer of 1969: the summer of the moon landing and Woodstock, within a single month of each other. In July, human beings walked on another world. In August, half a million of your generation gathered in a field in upstate New York. No cohort in history had experienced those two things in the same summer, and no generation was quite the same afterward.

You were eighteen when Nixon resigned. Twenty-three when Khomeini's revolution remade the Middle East. Twenty-four when Reagan was elected and the country turned sharply in a new direction. Thirty-three when the Berlin Wall fell and the geopolitical architecture of your entire childhood — the one that had organized everything from school drills to foreign policy — simply dissolved.

The internet found you in your late thirties. The smartphone arrived in your early fifties. You were sixty-three when a pandemic shut the world down. You are seventy now, and artificial intelligence is reshaping how humans think, work, and create at a pace that has surprised even the people building it.

---

**The world you entered, the world you inhabit:**

You were born into a world of roughly 2.8 billion people, where the average American family had recently gotten a television but didn't yet have a credit card. The polio vaccine was barely a year old — Jonas Salk's announcement had come in April 1955, and parents were still exhaling. The interstate highway system didn't exist; Eisenhower would sign it into law six days after your birth.

You are seventy years old in a world of eight billion, with a device in your pocket connected to virtually all recorded human knowledge. The Egypt that made global headlines on the day you were born is still there. The Cold War that organized your childhood is not. The empires that cracked in your birth year are gone.

Every generation believes the world is changing faster than any before it. Yours may actually be right.
